turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Karen, come on through. I'll grab your blood pressure before Doctor Nguyen sees you.

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, thanks. I was a bit early, the bus actually turned up, which it never does on a Tuesday, so I sat out there reading the flu-shot pamphlet and then the skin-check one, not that that's why I'm here.
[SEG0003] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Arm out straight for me. Blood pressure is one twenty-eight over seventy-eight, and your pulse is eighty-two.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that alright? I had a long black at the servo on the way, so it might be up a bit from the coffee, I always get nervous about that.
[SEG0005] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Temperature's thirty-six point eight, oxygen sats ninety-eight percent. He'll be with you in a tick.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Karen Hale. Have a seat. What's the problem?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the burning when I wee, again. It stings right at the end, and then I feel like I've got to go straight back, even when there's barely a trickle.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): This time, um, a few days. I want to say Tuesday, but it might've been the weekend. I honestly can't pin the day.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): Fever?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Not really though. I felt warm in bed, but the doona was up and the window was shut, so it might just have been that.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): Pain in your back?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No back pain at all. My lower tummy's been crampy, like period pain, and I'm not due for another fortnight.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Blood in the wee?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No red that I've seen. It looked a bit cloudy this morning, sort of hazy, but not bloody.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): How many times this year?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): This is the third. Well, actually, maybe the fourth. There was January, which I rode out, then March, then June, and now, so maybe four. I keep losing count, sorry.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Discharge or itch?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that. It's just the wee.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sexually active?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, with my partner, but not this week, it stings too much. We've been together two years, same bloke, and I felt embarrassed even saying the wee thing, let alone that.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): New partner?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I asked him this morning if he was sore or anything and he said no, over toast, which was mortifying.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): Nausea or vomiting?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Sometimes, not really. I went off my breakfast, but I didn't vomit. I think that's just me being anxious about coming in.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): What have you taken?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): I took some of my sister's leftover antibiotic. White capsules, the ones she had for her waterworks. I don't know the proper name, the bottle label was all smudged.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): How many?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Two a day, I think. Maybe it was one. I did that for two days and then I stopped, because it felt wrong taking someone else's, and I wasn't even sure they were in date.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Anything we prescribed?

[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): After the June one the other doctor gave me trimethoprim, a hundred milligrams, twice a day, for three days. I stopped it after the first day, back in June. It made me queasy and I didn't finish the pack.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Did you start the cephalexin script?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): No, I never got it from the chemist. I reckon the script's still in the glove box. I didn't take a single capsule.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): Anything from the chemist yourself?

[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): The urine sachets, the Ural ones, one sachet in water twice a day since yesterday. And Panadol, two tablets when the sting gets bad, which has been a couple of times a day.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): Medicine allergies?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing. I can take penicillin, I had it for a tooth years ago and I was fine.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any chance you're pregnant?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): No. My period was two weeks ago, normal, and we use condoms. I'm forty-two, so I do worry about it, but no, I'm not pregnant.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Keeping your fluids up?
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. I aim for a couple of litres, but yesterday I was out and I didn't really, so sometimes, not really.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll feel your tummy. Soft. No tenderness over the bladder to speak of, and no loin tenderness on either side.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): It still cramps when I actually wee, even if it doesn't hurt when you press. And, um, I wasn't totally straight with you before.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): About what?

[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): There is a bit of an itch, on the outside. And a little bit of creamy discharge, not heaps, just enough that I noticed it in my underwear this morning. I was embarrassed, so I said no.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any smell? Was sex sore before this week?
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): No bad smell. Sex was fine until the stinging started. The itch is new, last day or two, and it's mild.
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right. This sounds like another urine infection. With the itch I can't rule out thrush as well.

[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh. I did wonder if those white capsules stirred it up. My sister reckons antibiotics can do that, she read it, or maybe it was a podcast in the car, I can't remember which.
[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): Stop those. Don't take anyone else's antibiotics.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, I already stopped. I feel a bit stupid, honestly. Her dog had some vet drama and I ended up in her bathroom cabinet, which is a long story.
[SEG0052] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll get a urine sample today. Dip while you're here, and send a culture.

[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Do I have to wait for that before any tablets? Last time I was miserable for days, and I've got work tomorrow. I do the accounts for a little bakery in Marrickville, and month-end means a lot of sitting, which is hopeless when you're running to the loo.
[SEG0054] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sample first. If the culture grows something, I'll sort a script. No tablets from me today.
[SEG0055] person_3 (DOCTOR): If you're not better in three days, come back and see me. Sooner if you vomit, get a fever, or get pain in the loin.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): Three days, alright. And the cloudy wee, is that part of it? I keep checking the bowl, which is probably mad. My partner thinks I've lost the plot.
[SEG0057] person_3 (DOCTOR): It can be. The lab will tell us. Drink more water, and stick with your own Panadol and the Ural for now.

[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): The Ural tastes awful, like fizzy lemon gone wrong, but I'll keep at it. The Panadol is the ordinary one, five hundred milligrams, not the Osteo, two tablets like I said.
[SEG0059] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes. Two five-hundred-milligram tablets, up to four times a day if you need them. Don't go past eight tablets in a day.
[SEG0060] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Knock knock. I've got the specimen jar when you're ready.
[SEG0061] person_3 (DOCTOR): Thanks. Toilet's down the hall. She'll talk you through the sample.
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): Midstream, yeah, start then catch it. I always forget if I wipe first, and then I overthink it in the cubicle.
[SEG0063] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Wipe, wee a bit into the bowl, then into the jar, then finish in the bowl. Bring it straight back and I'll send it off.
[SEG0064] person_2 (PATIENT): If I can't go, because I get stage fright, do I just wait? I had two teas this morning so I should be right, but just in case.
[SEG0065] person_3 (DOCTOR): Wait, and have some water. We need that sample today.
[SEG0066] person_2 (PATIENT): Alright. And just so the notes are right, I'm not on the trimethoprim anymore, I stopped that in June, and I never started the cephalexin.
[SEG0067] person_3 (DOCTOR): Noted. Anything else?
[SEG0068] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Sorry I went on. I'll do the jar now.
[SEG0069] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Come with me and I'll show you the loo.
[SEG0070] person_3 (DOCTOR): Even if the dip looks obvious, I'll still wait on the culture before any script. Off you go.

spec.situation: Woman with burning urine again; says 'third time this year' then corrects to 'maybe the fourth'; took leftover antibiotic from a sister; embarrassed; vaginal symptoms denied, then partly admitted. Urine test ordered.
features: ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.

stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.

denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.

colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.

bad.reason: Cloudy urine supported, but severity 'mild' is not stated.
bad.text: cloudy urine (category=genitourinary, status=present, severity=mild, temporality=current, reported_by=patient, certainty=certain)

omissions.text: Urinary burning is specifically worse at the end of urination, with only barely a trickle when she feels she needs to go again.
Patient reported feeling warm in bed but was unsure if this represented fever; this possible fever history was not captured as uncertain.
No back pain at all was denied, and doctor later advised to return sooner for loin pain; recorded as back pain absent but the later red-flag wording is specifically loin pain.
This is the third or possibly fourth episode this year: January was ridden out, then March, then June, and now. The prior episode timing/count detail is not fully captured.
Initial denial of discharge/itch was corrected later; the transcript contains that the patient first said no because she was embarrassed.
Sexually active with same partner for two years; no new partner.
Partner reportedly had no soreness or symptoms.
She went off her breakfast but did not vomit; reduced appetite/feeling off breakfast was not recorded.
The borrowed antibiotic was explicitly her sister's leftover antibiotic and she stopped because it felt wrong and she was not sure it was in date.
Trimethoprim course in June was prescribed for 3 days, but she stopped after the first day and did not finish the pack. The recorded duration of 1 day misses that the prescribed duration was 3 days.
Cephalexin was prescribed previously but she never collected it from the chemist and did not take a single capsule.
No medicine allergies, with additional detail that she has tolerated penicillin previously.
Pregnancy denial included supporting details: last period was two weeks ago and normal, and they use condoms.
Fluid intake is inconsistent: she aims for a couple of litres but did not drink much yesterday.
Cramping occurs when she actually urinates even though pressing on the abdomen did not hurt.
The creamy discharge was only enough to notice in her underwear this morning.
No bad smell, and the itch is new over the last day or two and mild; only the odour and itch duration/severity are partly recorded, but the discharge timing 'noticed this morning' is not.
Doctor instructed that no tablets/antibiotics would be prescribed today, even if dip looks obvious, and that he would wait for the culture before any script.
Need for urine sample today was emphasized: if unable to void immediately, wait and drink some water because the sample is needed today.
